opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the more surprising things we saw when we were looking at the development of these small language models through the lens of susceptibilities and the local learning coefficient. Early in training, the model learns to predict common multigrams, things like n-grams of tokens that tend to co-occur, and initially a lot of that seems to be handled in the first layer. You can see this when you look at how different components respond to perturbations of the data distribution, which pieces of the network are "responsible" for which patterns.

But then, as training goes on, you see what looks like a migration. The multigram prediction stops being concentrated where it started, and more of it ends up being carried by later layers, or gets spread out. My interpretation, and I want to be careful because this is still an evolving picture, is that it reflects the model reorganizing its internal computation as it develops more sophisticated structure. Early on, the cheapest way to reduce loss is to memorize these local token patterns in whatever components are available. Later, once the model has built things like induction heads and other circuits that need that early-layer real estate, there's pressure to free up capacity, and the multigram computation gets moved or compressed into other parts of the network.

From the singular learning theory perspective, this is exactly the kind of thing we'd expect to see. Development isn't just accumulating new capabilities on top of old ones. The model moves between different regions of parameter space with different tradeoffs between loss and complexity, and when it transitions, the existing solutions can get restructured. So the migration was, in a way, a nice confirmation that you can't understand a trained model by looking only at its final state. The final location of a circuit doesn't tell you where it came from or why it's shaped the way it is, and the developmental history can be really informative for interpretability.

I'd also say it's a cautionary tale. If you did a single snapshot analysis at one checkpoint, you might conclude "layer one does multigrams" and then be confused later when that's no longer true. Tracking things over training gives you a much richer and, I think, more honest picture.

r001.rationale: It says multigram prediction becomes less concentrated in the first layer and shifts or spreads, but does not connect diverging layerwise learning-coefficient trends to loss of multigram-prediction information there.

r002.rationale: It does not describe path ablations or evidence that pattern prediction requires coordination between first- and second-layer heads.

r003.rationale: It presents migration as evidence of reorganization and as motivation for tracking development, but does not treat it as a lead for circuit discovery.

r004.rationale: It makes no prediction about migration signals appearing in larger models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the more surprising things that came out of that work. The context here is that we were looking at a small two-layer attention-only transformer, and we had this picture from the local learning coefficient, the refined LLC, that lets you look at how different parts of the model, different heads, different layers, are changing over training. And one of the structures we were tracking was this multigram circuit, which is basically the model learning to predict the next token from short sequences of previous tokens, n-gram-like statistics, but learned as a kind of distributed thing across the network.

And what we saw was that early in training, the multigram-relevant structure seemed to be concentrated in the first layer, and then over the course of training it looked like it was being handed off, like it moved to the second layer. The layer-one heads would start out specializing in this, and then they'd sort of relax, their LLC would drop or plateau, and the layer-two heads would pick it up.

So the question is, what do you make of that? And I think there are a couple of ways to interpret it. The naive interpretation is literally that the information migrates, that there's some mechanism by which the computation gets relocated. I don't think that's quite the right way to think about it, because gradient descent isn't doing anything so intentional. The better picture, I think, is in terms of the geometry of the loss landscape and the degeneracy of the model. Early on, the easiest place for the model to represent multigram statistics is wherever it happens to be cheapest in terms of the local structure of the landscape, and that turns out to be the first layer. But then as other circuits form, in particular the induction circuit, which needs the first layer to be doing previous-token work, there's a kind of competition for capacity. The first layer gets repurposed, and the multigram functionality gets pushed to wherever it can still live without interfering, which is layer two.

So I'd say it's less migration and more something like succession. One structure forms, another structure comes along that wants the same real estate, and the loss landscape reorganizes so that the earlier functionality gets re-expressed somewhere else. And the thing that was really nice about the LLC-based approach is that it let us see this happening without having to already know what we were looking for. We saw the geometric signature first, the change in the per-component learning coefficients, and then we went and did the mechanistic interpretability to confirm that yes, that's what the model is actually doing.

I'll be honest that we're still at the stage where some of this is suggestive rather than fully nailed down. There's a lot of degeneracy in these models, and it's genuinely hard to say "the multigram circuit is here" in a crisp way. But the fact that the geometry and the mechanistic story lined up as well as they did made me a lot more confident that these developmental tools are picking up on something real about how structure forms and gets reorganized during training.

r001.rationale: It says the first-layer heads’ LLC drops or plateaus as second-layer heads pick up the multigram functionality, describing a loss of that function in the first layer.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention path ablations or evidence that nested pattern prediction requires coordination between first- and second-layer heads.

r003.rationale: It says the geometric signature appeared first and led them to mechanistic interpretability to confirm the circuit, treating the apparent shift as a discovery lead.

r004.rationale: It makes no prediction about whether migration signals will appear in larger models.

astra-6.text:
My interpretation was that it wasn’t necessarily the information moving so much as the computation being reorganized. A multigram circuit has to recognize a particular sequence of tokens and use that to influence the prediction. There can be different ways of distributing that work across layers, so a signal becoming weaker in one layer and stronger in another could reflect a change in how the model implements the same behavior.

But I’d be cautious about calling that migration based just on where we could detect the information. There’s a difference between information being present and the model actually using it. To establish that the computation had moved, we’d want causal evidence that the later layers had taken over the role the earlier layers were playing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible redistribution of computation, but does not mention diverging learning-coefficient trends or a loss of information in the first layer.

r002.rationale: It does not describe path ablations or coordination between first- and second-layer heads.

r003.rationale: It treats the apparent layerwise shift as a reason to investigate whether computation moved, calling for causal evidence to establish that.

r004.rationale: It makes no prediction about migration signals appearing more generally in larger models.

sol-6.1.text:
My interpretation was that we were seeing information being moved around, rather than the model independently learning the same multigram at each layer. A multigram here is a sequence of tokens that’s useful for predicting what comes next. One layer might recognize part of that sequence, and a later layer might combine that with more context or turn it into a prediction.

But I’d be cautious about calling it a literal migration. Where you can detect information isn’t necessarily where the computation responsible for using it happens. The representation can change between layers, so something that looks like it disappears in one place and reappears in another could partly reflect how we’re measuring it. To establish the stronger claim, you’d want interventions showing that the later representation actually depends on the earlier one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses information appearing to disappear and reappear across layers, but does not connect diverging learning-coefficient trends to a loss of multigram-prediction information in the first layer.

r002.rationale: It does not mention path ablations or coordination between first-layer and second-layer heads.

r003.rationale: It interprets apparent migration and suggests interventions to test it, but does not describe migration as a lead for circuit discovery.

r004.rationale: It makes no prediction about migration signals appearing in larger models.
